sectionImages.creator: Roberto Fortuna, for the National Museum of Denmark
sectionImages.date: photographed 2010; the stone raised about 965
sectionImages.note: The earliest Scandinavian royal statement of Christianisation, and a boast by the interested party rather than a description of a completed conversion. The runic text records that Harald had the monument made in memory of Gorm his father and Þyrvé his mother, and describes himself as the Harald who won for himself all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian. Studio lighting, colour, stone filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: The iron helmet from the Gjermundbu grave in Ringerike, Norway, from a burial of about 950 to 1000, photographed in 2010 at the NTNU Vitenskapsmuseet.
sectionImages.creator: NTNU Vitenskapsmuseet (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 2010; the helmet from a grave of about 950 to 1000
sectionImages.note: The only substantially preserved helmet from Viking-Age Scandinavia, and the direct answer to the horned-helmet myth: a rounded cap of four riveted plates with a spectacle guard over the eyes, and no horns of any kind. Nothing in the Viking-Age corpus or in contemporary depictions shows a horned war helmet. The word cropped in the filename means the photograph was tightened onto the object. Licensed CC BY 2.0.

sectionImages.caption: The Lögberg, the Law Rock, at Þingvellir in Iceland, photographed in June 2008. The Alþingi met here each summer from about 930, and the lawspeaker recited the law aloud from memory.
sectionImages.creator: Panoramio contributor (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 28 June 2008
sectionImages.note: The site rather than a reconstruction: a rift-valley wall that gave an open-air assembly the acoustics of a natural amphitheatre. The exact position of the Lögberg within Þingvellir is debated, and the flagpole in the photograph marks the traditional identification rather than an excavated one. Colour, 700 by 467 pixels, which is modest but adequate at section-image size. Licensed CC BY 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: The carved north portal of Urnes stave church on the Sognefjord, photographed in 2016. The woodwork was made about 1070 and reused in the present church.
sectionImages.creator: Bjørn Erik Pedersen (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 10 August 2016; the carving made about 1070
sectionImages.note: The type object of the Urnes style, the last and most refined phase of Norse animal art: elegantly thin animals in figure-of-eight loops, carved for a Christian building. It is the clearest single illustration of what the conversion did to Norse art, which was to continue it rather than end it. Colour, high resolution, the carving filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.caption: A modern map of Scandinavian settlement and voyaging between the eighth and eleventh centuries, drawn in 2007. Shading marks settlement by century; green marks coasts raided but never settled.
sectionImages.creator: Max Naylor (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: drawn 24 June 2007
sectionImages.note: The reach described in this section, shown at once: the Faroes, Iceland, Greenland and Vinland to the west, the Rus' river routes and the Volga Bulgars to the east, and the Danelaw, Normandy and the Irish port towns between. The map is a modern reconstruction of settlement zones rather than a medieval document, and the green raided-only areas are approximate. Colour, legend legible at section size. Released into the public domain by its author.

sectionImages.caption: The opening page of the Peterborough Chronicle, a manuscript of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle written in Old English about 1121. English annalists called the Scandinavians Dene and hæþene men, never vikings.
sectionImages.creator: Anonymous twelfth-century scribe at Peterborough
sectionImages.date: the manuscript written about 1121
sectionImages.source: Wikimedia Commons (Bodleian Library, Oxford, MS Laud Misc. 636)
sectionImages.note: The outsiders' vocabulary this section describes, in the hand of one of the outsiders. The Chronicle applies Dene, Danes, to Scandinavians of any origin, so its Danes of Northumbria may well have been Norwegians, and elsewhere it identifies them by religion rather than by any ethnic name. The inscription at the foot records the manuscript's later ownership by Archbishop Laud in 1638. Colour, the page filling the frame. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: The iron helmet from boat grave 1 at Vendel in Uppland, Sweden, made in the seventh century and photographed in 2008 at the Swedish History Museum in Stockholm.
sectionImages.creator: Mararie (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 4 January 2008; the helmet from a boat grave of the seventh century
sectionImages.note: The warrior elite that emerged from the post-536 recovery, and the direct comparandum for Sutton Hoo named in this section: crest, eyebrow ridges and decorated panels of the same North Sea tradition. Vendel and Valsgärde are the type sites for the period that precedes and produces the Viking Age, which is why this article's Origins section begins here rather than at 793. Colour, the object large in the frame against a dark ground. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.

sectionImages.caption: The coast of the Nappstraumen strait on Flakstadøya in Lofoten, northern Norway, photographed in April 2017. This is the sheltered inner lead that gave Norðvegr, the north way, its name.
sectionImages.creator: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen)
sectionImages.date: photographed 6 April 2017
sectionImages.note: The geography this section argues from: thin arable ground at the water's edge, mountains immediately behind, and a protected channel running inside the islands that made a coastal voyage safer than an overland one. A country named after a shipping route is a country organised by ships. Colour, high resolution. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.caption: The stone church at Hvalsey in the Eastern Settlement of Norse Greenland, built in the fourteenth century and photographed in 2014. A wedding here in 1408 is the last documented event in Norse Greenland.
sectionImages.creator: Number 57 (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 3 August 2014; the church built in the fourteenth century
sectionImages.note: The far end of the North Atlantic colonisation described here, and the best-preserved Norse building in Greenland: mortarless stone standing nearly to the wall-head. The 1408 wedding is attested not in Greenland but in letters written in Iceland shortly afterwards, which is why it is the last securely documented moment rather than the last event. Colour, the ruin filling the frame. Released CC0.

sectionImages.caption: An aerial photograph taken in 2008 of the ring fortress at Trelleborg on Zealand, Denmark, whose timbers were felled in 980 and 981. Four gates at the cardinal points open through a perfectly circular rampart.
sectionImages.creator: Thue C. Leibrandt (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 15 February 2008; the fortress built in 980 and 981
sectionImages.note: The clearest physical measure of what Harald Bluetooth's authority could actually do, and the reason this section treats Denmark as consolidating first: an exact geometric survey executed at five sites across the realm within two building seasons. The internal divisions visible inside the rampart mark the squares of longhouses. Colour, the whole fortress in the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: A reconstructed warp-weighted loom in house 2 at the Hedeby Viking Museum in Schleswig, photographed in 2008. Weaving of this kind produced both a household's cloth and every sail a ship carried.
sectionImages.creator: Kai-Erik Ballak (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 1 November 2008; the loom a modern museum reconstruction
sectionImages.note: A modern reconstruction, not an excavated object: the looms themselves were wood and have not survived, and what archaeology recovers is the fired clay loom weights hanging along the warp here. The point this section makes is visible in the scale of it — a single large sail took years of this work, so the ships rested on women's labour as surely as on shipwrights'. Colour, the loom filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.section: Rank, and the people who were owned
sectionImages.caption: A leaf of the Codex Wormianus, the Icelandic manuscript of about 1350 that preserves Rígsþula, the Eddic poem dividing society into slave, farmer and noble.
sectionImages.creator: Anonymous Icelandic scribe; digitised for Wikimedia Commons
sectionImages.date: the manuscript written about 1350
sectionImages.note: The source for the three-rank scheme this section opens with. The leaf reproduced is folio 13r, from the manuscript's text of Snorri's Edda rather than from Rígsþula itself, so it stands for the codex rather than for the poem's page. It is offered as the manuscript witness and not as evidence for slavery, which rests instead on the law codes, on Dublin and Hedeby as markets, and on Ibn Fadlan's eyewitness list of enslaved girls among Rus' merchants' goods on the Volga in 922. No photograph of a securely dated Viking-Age slave collar or fetter could be sourced on Wikimedia Commons. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: The Ledberg runestone beside Ledberg church in Östergötland, Sweden, carved in the eleventh century and photographed in 2009. Armed men with helmets, shields and spears fill the registers above a ship.
sectionImages.creator: Phlanx (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 20 June 2009; the stone carved in the eleventh century
sectionImages.note: A contemporary Scandinavian depiction of armed men, which the sagas are not: helmeted figures with round shields and spears, and a ship at the base, carved by people who had seen both. The carving is filled with modern red pigment to make the lines legible, a standard conservation practice on Swedish runestones and not original colour. The lowest figure, attacked by a beast at the foot, is often read as a Ragnarök scene. Colour, the stone filling the frame. Licensed CC BY 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: A silver Thor's hammer pendant with filigree ornament from Scania in southern Sweden, made in the tenth century and photographed in 2011 at the Swedish History Museum.
sectionImages.creator: The Swedish History Museum, Stockholm
sectionImages.date: photographed 2 November 2011; the pendant made in the tenth century
sectionImages.note: The amulet this section describes as very plausibly a deliberate counterpart to the cross, worn as hammers multiply through the tenth century. The museum records the find spot only as Scania, without a parish, so the object is provenanced to a province rather than to a site. The soapstone mould from Trendgården in Jutland, which casts hammers and crosses side by side, is the sharpest evidence that the two were being made for the same market. Colour, the object large on a plain ground. Licensed CC BY 2.0.

sectionImages.caption: The Rök runestone in Östergötland, Sweden, raised in the early ninth century and photographed in 2009. Its roughly 700 runes make it the longest known runic inscription.
sectionImages.creator: Bengt Olof Åradsson (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 19 November 2009; the stone raised in the early ninth century
sectionImages.note: Writing as this section describes it: carved by a man who spoke the language, in the sixteen-character Younger Futhark that had just replaced the twenty-four-character Elder Futhark. The inscription, raised by Varinn in memory of his son Vamoðr, uses cipher runes and allusive verse whose meaning is still argued over. The red infill is modern conservation pigment, not original. Colour, the stone filling the frame. Licensed CC BY 1.0.

sectionImages.caption: Hacksilver from the Spillings hoard, buried on Gotland in the 870s and photographed in 2015 at Gotlands Museum in Visby. Arm-rings were cut into fragments and weighed rather than counted.
sectionImages.creator: W.carter (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 19 April 2015; the silver buried in the 870s
sectionImages.note: The bullion economy of this section in physical form. The Spillings hoard, found in 1999, is the largest Viking silver hoard known at about sixty-seven kilograms, and the cut and nicked pieces here show the two tests a trader applied: cut to make a weighable fragment, nick to check the metal was silver through. Much of the coin in such hoards is Islamic dirham silver that came north up the Volga. Colour, the objects filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

sectionImages.caption: Reconstructed Viking-age houses at Hedeby on the Schlei inlet in Schleswig, photographed in April 2006. The town stood where cargo crossed the neck of Jutland between the Baltic and the North Sea.
sectionImages.creator: Caravaca (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 16 April 2006; the buildings modern reconstructions on the excavated site
sectionImages.note: Modern reconstructions built on the excavated plots, not surviving buildings, with the plank walkway and wattle fences following the excavated layout. Hedeby's position is the whole point: goods moved overland across the narrow base of Jutland instead of sailing the long and dangerous passage around Skagen. The town held a harbour, a mint, workshops and one of northern Europe's principal slave markets behind a semicircular rampart. Colour, the buildings filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.5.

sectionImages.caption: The reconstructed chieftain's hall at Borg in Lofoten, northern Norway, photographed in March 2019. The excavated building it copies ran about eighty-three metres, the largest Norse longhouse known.
sectionImages.creator: Christoph Strässler (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 13 March 2019; the reconstruction of a hall of the ninth and tenth centuries
sectionImages.note: A full-scale reconstruction rather than a surviving building, raised beside the excavated post-holes it is based on. It shows the three-aisled longhouse form this section describes — bowed walls, a single ridge running the length of the building, the roof carried on two internal rows of posts — at the top of the size range; an ordinary farm was about a fifth as long. Colour, the whole building in the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.

sectionImages.caption: Hjalmar Stolpe's engraved plan of Birka chamber grave Bj 581, published in 1889. It records a sword, axe, spear, shields, arrows, two horses and a gaming set laid out around the body.
sectionImages.creator: Evald Hansen, after the excavation drawings of Hjalmar Stolpe
sectionImages.date: published 1889; the grave excavated in 1878
sectionImages.note: The document the whole argument rests on, and the reason the grave was read as a male warrior's for over a century. What the plan establishes is the assemblage and its arrangement: the complete equipment of a mounted commander, including the gaming board and pieces generally read as a marker of tactical command. It does not establish who used any of it. The 2017 genomic analysis and the 2019 follow-up in Antiquity showed the individual was biologically female and that the buriers intended the commander's reading; neither shows that she fought, and the 2019 paper says so explicitly. Monochrome because the only record of the excavated layout is this engraving. Public domain.

sectionImages.caption: A surviving stretch of the Danevirke rampart in Schleswig, photographed in March 2007. The earthwork closed the Jutland isthmus against Frankish and later German pressure from the south.
sectionImages.creator: Joachim Müllerchen (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 4 March 2007; the rampart's main phase built in 737
sectionImages.note: The physical form of the relationship this section opens with. Denmark was the only part of the Norse world with a land frontier, and the Danevirke is what a land frontier required: its main phase is dated by felled timbers to 737, decades before Lindisfarne and two generations before Charlemagne reached the Danish border. King Godfred reinforced it when he confronted the Franks. Colour, the earthwork filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 2.0 de.

sectionImages.section: Becoming Danes, Normans, Rus and English
sectionImages.caption: Lund Cathedral in Skåne, then Danish, consecrated in 1145 and photographed in 2011. Lund had become the archbishopric for all Scandinavia in 1103 or 1104.
sectionImages.creator: Forea.shakil (Wikimedia Commons)
sectionImages.date: photographed 24 May 2011; the cathedral consecrated in 1145
sectionImages.note: What joining Latin Europe looked like in stone. An archbishopric at Lund meant Scandinavia was no longer mission territory administered from Hamburg-Bremen, and the Romanesque cathedral raised to go with it belongs to the same generation as the tithes, the written law in Latin letters and the royal coinage. Nidaros followed in 1152 or 1153 and Uppsala in 1164. Colour, the building filling the frame. Licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.

sectionImages.caption: Carl Emil Doepler's wood engraving of Odin enthroned, published in 1882. Doepler designed the costumes for the first complete Ring cycle at Bayreuth in 1876, and the winged helmet is his invention rather than a Norse object.
sectionImages.creator: Carl Emil Doepler (1824–1905)
sectionImages.date: published 1882
sectionImages.source: Wikimedia Commons (Wilhelm Wägner, Nordisch-germanische Götter und Helden, 1882)
sectionImages.note: The invention caught in the act, by the man most responsible for it. Doepler dressed Wagner's gods and heroes at Bayreuth in 1876 and then illustrated Wägner's popular mythology handbook six years later, and the winged helmet here has no Viking-Age precedent of any kind — no find and no contemporary depiction shows a horned or winged war helmet. Monochrome because the original is a nineteenth-century wood engraving; a colour version does not exist. Public domain.
